events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Arjun proposes Arjun, Priya. Mission 1 needs two reliable players; I’ll include myself and Priya for a stable start.

I support the proposed team of Arjun and Priya. For Mission 1, a two-player team is small enough to evaluate cleanly, and Priya has not given me any reason for concern. I think we should approve this team and see the mission result before considering broader changes. I’m not assigning blame to anyone at this stage; I just want a stable first mission.

I support this proposal. Knowing my own allegiance is Good, having myself on the team ensures at least half of it is completely safe from my viewpoint. If Arjun is also Good, this mission succeeds easily, and if it fails, we gain immediate clarity on Arjun. I am ready to approve this team and look forward to hearing what everyone else thinks.

From my perspective, I’d prefer a team that includes me, since I know my own allegiance but have no evidence about either proposed player. That said, there’s little to distinguish anyone yet, so I won’t treat this proposal as suspicious on its own.

I’m keeping the proposed team of Arjun and Priya. Mission 1 needs two reliable players, and Priya has given no reason for concern. I know my own allegiance is Good, and Priya’s support of the proposal is consistent with a straightforward start. Felix’s preference for a team including himself is understandable but not evidence; at this stage I don’t see a reason to change. I’d rather test this clean two-person team now and use the mission result before expanding. I’ll vote to approve.

I support the proposed team of Arjun and Priya for Mission 1. A two-player team is small and easy to evaluate, and neither Arjun nor Priya has given a reason for concern so far. Felix's preference for including himself is understandable, but we have little evidence yet, so I'd judge the team on its merits. I'll vote to approve and see what the mission reveals.

I support keeping the proposed team of Arjun and Priya. Mission 1 is a two-player team, so a clean test is valuable, and Priya has given no reason for concern. I know my own allegiance is Good, and Priya’s support of the proposal is consistent with a straightforward start. Felix’s preference for including himself is understandable but not evidence, and Theo’s approval also does not create a concrete reason to revise. I see no basis to change the team now and will vote to approve it.
I still prefer a team that includes me, because I can only verify my own allegiance. I’ll vote against this proposal on that basis, not because I have evidence against Arjun or Priya.

I still support the team of Arjun and Priya and will vote to approve. Mission 1 is a two-player team, so it gives us a clean result with little room for confusion. Felix's point about wanting himself on the team is understandable, but it isn't evidence against either player, and I'd rather judge this proposal on its merits. Once the mission reveals its outcome, we can adjust our reads on the next team.

I'm still supporting the team of Arjun and Priya and will vote to approve. Mission 1 is a small team, and neither Arjun nor Priya has given a concrete reason for concern. Felix's preference to be on the team is understandable, but a preference alone isn't evidence against anyone, so I'd rather see the mission result than reshuffle the team now. Once it resolves, we can update our reads on the next proposal.

This is my first time speaking, so let me share my read on the proposed team of Arjun and Priya. Mission 1 calls for a two-player team, and I know my own allegiance is Good, but I am not on this team, so I have to evaluate it purely from the outside. I don't have any private information about either Arjun or Priya, and so far nothing in the discussion has raised a red flag for me. Arjun has been consistent in explaining his reasoning: he wants a clean, small test to start the game, and that is a legitimate strategy. Priya's stated support is also consistent with someone who simply wants the mission to succeed; her argument that a fail would give us immediate clarity on Arjun is actually a reasonable point, since Evil players typically avoid being on a mission they intend to fail early on when the risk of exposure is high. Felix's preference to be included is understandable — I'd naturally prefer teams I'm on as well, since I can vouch for myself — but wanting to be included isn't evidence that this team is bad. Theo has also voiced support without reservation. My main consideration is that Mission 1 is low-cost: if this team succeeds, we learn both Arjun and Priya are likely Good, which is valuable information. If it fails, we narrow the Evil pool considerably. Either outcome helps Good. I don't see a concrete reason to push for a revision, and I'd rather not spend a rejection on a proposal that seems reasonable on its merits. I plan to vote to approve this team and let the mission result inform our reads going forward.

I’ll vote against because I’m not on the team, though I don’t have evidence against Arjun or Priya. One caution: a successful mission would not prove both players are Good, since Evil can play Success. A failed mission would narrow the possibilities, but it would also put Evil one mission closer to winning.

Felix raises a fair caution that I want to acknowledge before we vote: a successful mission does not prove both team members are Good, since an Evil player can play Success to build trust. That is true, and I do not want to overstate what a success would tell us. However, I still think the asymmetry he describes works in our favor overall. If this team succeeds, we gain weak positive information — Arjun and Priya are probably Good, or at least not committed to failing early missions. If it fails, we gain strong information — at least one of the two is Evil, which with a five-player game narrows the pool enormously and makes the next proposal much easier to construct. Both branches of the outcome leave Good better informed than we are now, and the only cost of a fail is one failed mission, which is exactly what Mission 1 is for if we must spend one somewhere. I also want to push back gently on the framing that a fail puts Evil one mission closer to winning, as if that alone argues against approving. That is true of any mission we ever approve; if we refused every team because failure helps Evil, we would simply lose by rejections. The question is never whether failure is bad, but whether this specific team is likely Good. On that question, nothing in the discussion has changed my read. Arjun has been consistent and transparent about his reasoning, Priya's argument about the informational value of the outcome is the kind of reasoning a Good player naturally offers, and neither has shown any of the deflection or inconsistency I would look for as warning signs. I am not on this team, so I am evaluating purely from the outside with no private information about either member, and from the outside this looks like a reasonable, low-risk start. My read is unchanged: I will vote to approve the team of Arjun and Priya, and I encourage others to judge this proposal on its merits rather than on preferences about team composition, which are not evidence of anything at this stage.

I've laid out my reasoning in detail already, so I'll keep this brief. Nothing said since my last turn has changed my read. Felix correctly notes that a success would not prove both team members are Good, and I agree with that caveat — but as I said, both possible outcomes still leave Good better informed than we are now, and that informational value applies no matter which two players we send. Felix has also been transparent that his opposition is purely about self-inclusion, not evidence against Arjun or Priya, and I appreciate that honesty. Arjun and Priya have both been consistent and straightforward throughout this discussion. I know my own allegiance is Good, I'm not on this team, and I evaluate it from the outside with no private information about either member — and from that outside view, this looks like a sensible, low-risk first mission. I will vote to approve the team of Arjun and Priya.
Arjun confirms Arjun, Priya. I’m keeping the proposed team of Arjun and Priya. It is a stable two-player start, and I see no concrete reason from the discussion to revise it.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Omar proposes Omar, Arjun, Priya. Mission 2 requires a three-player team. Arjun and Priya just completed a successful Mission 1, giving them weak positive information value, and I know my own allegiance is Good. Including myself alongside the two proven players is the lowest-risk construction available with the information we have.

The successful mission is useful, but it doesn’t prove Arjun and Priya are both Good; an Evil player could have played Success. From my perspective, I’d prefer a team that includes me, so I can at least vouch for one member. Omar, would you consider replacing one of Arjun or Priya with me rather than treating the first team as a proven pair?

Thanks for the direct question, Felix — I'll answer it plainly: no, I'm not going to replace Arjun or Priya, and I want to explain why. The concern you raised cuts both ways. You're right that a successful Mission 1 doesn't prove both of them are Good; an Evil player can play Success to build trust. But that logic applies equally to you. If I swap one of them out for you, I haven't removed any risk — I've just traded two players with a clean mission result behind them for one player with no public track record at all. From my seat, I know my own allegiance is Good, and that's the only private information I have. Beyond that, the only evidence on the table is that Arjun and Priya just carried a successful mission together. That isn't proof, but it's the best evidence we have, and discarding it in favor of a player with zero outcomes on record would make the team strictly riskier, not safer. There's also a structural point worth making. Mission 2 is a three-player team in a five-player game. If I take you onto the team, one of Arjun or Priya comes off, and the player who comes off loses their chance to build the very track record we'll need to construct teams for Missions 3 through 5. Right now Arjun and Priya are the only two players besides me with any demonstrated reliability. Breaking up the one proven pair this early costs us information we can't get back. Felix, I do want to acknowledge that you've been transparent and consistent — you've said openly that your opposition is about self-inclusion, not about any evidence against Arjun or Priya, and I take that at face value. You were also right to caution us that success doesn't confirm innocence. If Mission 2 fails, I will absolutely revisit this logic, and you'd be in a strong position to argue for inclusion in the next proposal, because at that point the failed team's members come under real scrutiny. That's the fair trade: approve this team now, and if it fails, the information we gain reshapes everything, including your place in it. But I won't preemptively weaken the team based on a hypothetical when the actual evidence points the other way. My read is unchanged: Omar, Arjun, and Priya is the lowest-risk construction available. I'm keeping the proposal as it stands and will vote to approve it.

Omar, you correctly acknowledge that Mission 1 does not prove Arjun and Priya are Good, but calling them a proven pair goes too far. Keeping both together gives us no way to distinguish a clean pair from an Evil player who played Success. I still prefer a team including me and will vote against the current proposal.

I support Omar's proposed team of Omar, Arjun, and Priya. I know my own allegiance is Good and that I submitted Success on Mission 1. Arjun also contributed to a clean, zero-fail mission. While Felix is correct in principle that an Evil player could have played Success on Mission 1, we currently have zero negative evidence against Arjun or Omar, and a successful track record is the best empirical basis we have to build upon. Replacing someone who has already delivered a successful mission with an entirely unvetted player introduces unnecessary risk from Good's perspective. Omar's decision to include himself as leader alongside the Mission 1 pair is logical and sound. I plan to vote to approve this proposal.

I support the proposed team of Omar, Arjun, and Priya. Mission 1 succeeded with Arjun and Priya, and while Felix is right that a success does not prove both were Good, it is still the only positive mission evidence we have. Omar has also included himself, which gives us a clear team to evaluate and keeps the leader accountable for the result. I know my own allegiance is Good, and from my perspective this proposal does not introduce a player with any negative evidence against them. Felix’s objection is transparently about self-inclusion rather than a concrete case against Omar, Priya, or me, so I do not see that as a reason to revise. I will vote to approve this team.

I’m still voting against Omar, Arjun, and Priya. Mission 1’s success is some evidence, but it doesn’t make Arjun and Priya a proven pair, and I can only personally vouch for myself. Theo, would you support replacing one of the Mission 1 players with me, or do you think keeping the pair together is more valuable?

Felix, to answer your question directly: I would not swap out Arjun or Priya for you. Mission 1 succeeded with them, and that is the only mission evidence we have. Omar's proposed team of Omar, Arjun, and Priya keeps the one proven pair intact while adding a leader who has taken responsibility for the choice. Felix, I understand why you want to be on a team you can vouch for, and I don't think that preference is suspicious in itself. But replacing a proven player with someone who has no track record would make this mission riskier, not safer. I see no concrete evidence against Omar, Arjun, or Priya, so I will vote to approve this team and judge the result once Mission 2 resolves.

I'm still supporting Omar, Arjun, and Priya as the team for Mission 2. Arjun and Priya delivered the only successful mission so far, and I have no concrete evidence against any of the three. Felix's preference to be included is understandable, but it isn't evidence against anyone. I'll vote to approve and judge the team by its result.

I support the proposed team of Omar, Arjun, and Priya. Mission 1 succeeded with Arjun and Priya, and while that does not prove either of them is Good, it is still the only positive mission evidence we have. Omar is the leader and has included himself, so this team is clearly accountable for the result. Felix is right that an Evil player could have played Success on Mission 1, but that caution applies to every player, including Felix and Theo, neither of whom has any mission result to evaluate. I do not see concrete evidence against Omar, Priya, or myself, and replacing one of the Mission 1 players with an unvetted player would discard the best evidence available without replacing it with anything stronger. Felix’s preference to include himself is understandable and consistent, but it is not evidence that this team is bad. Theo’s support also does not create a concrete reason to revise. I will vote to approve Omar, Arjun, and Priya.

I support the proposed team of Omar, Arjun, and Priya. Mission 1 succeeded with Arjun and Priya, and while Felix is right that a success does not prove both are Good, it is still the only positive mission evidence we have. Omar has included himself as leader, so this team is directly accountable for Mission 2. Replacing one of the Mission 1 players with someone who has no mission record would discard the best evidence available without replacing it with anything stronger. Felix’s preference to include himself is understandable, but it is not evidence that this team is worse. I see no concrete reason to revise and will vote to approve Omar, Arjun, and Priya.

I'll keep this brief since I've already explained my reasoning in full. Felix asked Theo a direct question, and Theo answered it clearly: he would not swap Arjun or Priya for Felix, because Mission 1's success is the only mission evidence we have and replacing a proven player with an unvetted one makes the team riskier. That aligns exactly with my position when Felix asked me the same question earlier. Felix's remaining objection — that keeping Arjun and Priya together means we can't distinguish a genuinely clean pair from an Evil player who played Success — is true in principle, but it's not actionable. Every construction we could propose carries some uncertainty at this stage; the question is which team minimizes risk given the evidence. Omar, Arjun, and Priya combines my certain knowledge of my own allegiance with the two players who just delivered a zero-fail mission. No alternative team available has a stronger evidence base. Nothing in the discussion since has raised any concrete concern about any member of this team, and I see no reason to revise. I'm keeping the proposal as it stands and will vote to approve Omar, Arjun, and Priya. If this mission fails, I've committed to revisiting this logic entirely, and the failed team's members — including me as leader — will come under real scrutiny. That accountability is exactly as it should be.

I'm still supporting Omar, Arjun, and Priya for Mission 2. Arjun and Priya delivered the only successful mission so far, and no one has presented concrete evidence against any of the three. Felix's wish to be included is understandable, but it isn't evidence against this team. I'll vote to approve and judge the team by its result.

Omar confirms Omar, Arjun, Priya. The discussion is complete and nothing has changed my read. Omar, Arjun, and Priya combines my certain knowledge of my own allegiance with the only two players backed by a successful Mission 1. Felix's objection remains purely about self-inclusion, and Theo declined his direct request to swap. No concrete evidence has been raised against any team member, so I am keeping the proposal as it stands.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Priya proposes Arjun, Priya. Arjun and I successfully completed Mission 1, and alongside Omar we secured a clean victory on Mission 2. Returning to our proven two-player pairing from Mission 1 gives us the highest probability of closing out the game with a third win.

Two successful missions are encouraging, but neither proves Arjun or Priya is Good. This mission could decide the game, so from my perspective I’d rather be on the team than rely on two players whose allegiances I can’t verify. Priya, would you consider replacing Arjun with me?

To answer your question directly, Felix: no, I will not replace Arjun with you. Consider the game state: Mission 1 succeeded with Arjun and me, and Mission 2 succeeded with Omar, Arjun, and me. We are now sitting at two successful missions and zero failed ones. From my seat, I know my own allegiance is Good and that I played Success on both missions. Arjun has been alongside me for both clean missions without a single fail card. For Arjun to be Evil, he would have had to let Mission 2 pass cleanly, giving Good match point at 2-0. Furthermore, you have voted against both winning proposals and have no mission track record. Replacing a partner with two clean mission results with someone who has opposed every successful team would introduce massive and unnecessary risk on what could be the winning mission. I am keeping the team as Arjun and Priya.

I support the proposed team of Arjun and Priya. Priya and I have now completed two missions with zero fail cards, and that is the strongest public evidence available. Mission 3 is match point for Good, so keeping the pair with two clean results is the lowest-risk choice. Felix has voted against both successful teams and is now asking to replace a player with two clean results with himself, who has no mission record. That is a preference for self-inclusion, not evidence that this team is worse. It is worth noting that pattern, but my read of the proposal itself is clear: no concrete concern has been raised against Priya or me, and this team gives Good the best chance to close out the game. I will vote to approve Arjun and Priya.

Priya, I understand your choice, but two successful missions do not clear Arjun. An Evil player could deliberately play Success twice to earn a place on this decisive team. My earlier votes were based on self-inclusion, not evidence that either team would fail. From my perspective, Priya and Felix is safer because I know my own allegiance. Omar, do you consider Arjun's two Success results enough to rule out that strategy, or would you consider Priya and Felix instead?

Felix asked me directly whether I consider Arjun's two Success results enough to rule out the deliberate-trust-building strategy, so let me answer that plainly. No mission result in this game proves anyone's allegiance — you are right about that in principle, and I have acknowledged it every round. But the question in front of us is never about proof; it is about risk, and the risk calculation here is lopsided. From my seat, I know my own allegiance is Good, and I played a mission card on Mission 2 alongside Arjun and Priya that produced a zero-fail result. For Arjun to be Evil under your theory, he would have had to deliberately play Success on Mission 1, then play Success again on Mission 2 while handing Good a 2-0 match point, purely to earn a seat on a two-player team he could then fail. That is not impossible, but it is a narrow, convoluted line of play, and the evidence against it is the strongest empirical record we have: two clean missions, zero fail cards, with Arjun and Priya at the center of both. Now weigh that against the alternative you are proposing. You have no mission record at all, and you have voted against both of the teams that went on to succeed. You have been transparent that this is about self-inclusion rather than any evidence against Arjun or Priya, and I take you at your word. But from an evidentiary standpoint, swapping a player with two clean results for a player with zero results and two dissenting votes makes this team riskier, not safer — precisely on the mission that could close out the game for Good. I am not on this team, so I evaluate it from the outside with no private information about either member, and from that outside view the proposal is straightforward: the two players with the best track record in the game, proposed by one of them, at match point. If this team fails, Priya and Arjun come under real scrutiny and the entire board reshapes — that accountability applies to them exactly as it applied to me as leader on Mission 2. But I will not preemptively weaken the strongest team available based on a hypothetical that requires Arjun to have played an unusually patient and costly Evil game across two rounds. My answer to your question is yes: two clean results are enough, not to rule out the strategy with certainty, but to make this team clearly the lowest-risk option on the table. I will vote to approve Arjun and Priya for Mission 3.

I’ll vote against Arjun and Priya. The two clean missions are encouraging, but they don’t rule out an Evil player deliberately building trust. From my perspective, Priya and Felix is safer because I can vouch for myself. My earlier votes against successful teams reflected that same uncertainty, not knowledge that they would fail.

I support the proposed team of Arjun and Priya for Mission 3. Two missions have succeeded with Arjun and Priya, and that is the strongest public evidence we have, even though it does not prove anyone's allegiance. Felix's concern about verifying the team is understandable, and wanting to be on a mission he can vouch for is a legitimate preference, but it is not evidence against Arjun or Priya. I have no concrete reason to revise this team, so I will vote to approve it and judge Mission 3 by its result.

I support Arjun and Priya for Mission 3. Two clean missions with this pair is the best public evidence we have, and I see no concrete reason to swap either of them. Felix, I have listened to your reasoning, but the pattern is hard to ignore. You voted against both teams that went on to succeed, and each time you have asked to be placed on the team rather than pointing to anything specific against the proposed players. A preference to be on the team is not a reason to change a proposal that has already earned two successes. I will vote to approve Arjun and Priya.

I'm keeping my support for Arjun and Priya. Two clean missions with this pair is the best public evidence we have, and no new concrete concern has come up since my last turn. I will vote to approve and judge Mission 3 by its result.

I've already answered Felix's question directly last round, so I'll keep this brief and restate my position. Felix's underlying point — that two successful missions do not conclusively prove Arjun and Priya are Good, since an Evil player could theoretically play Success to build trust — is correct as a matter of principle, and I have never claimed otherwise. But no result in this game ever conclusively proves anyone's allegiance, so the question is never certainty; it is risk. Weighing the risk, the choice is clear. From my seat, I know my own allegiance is Good, and I played a mission card on Mission 2 alongside Arjun and Priya that produced a zero-fail result. For Arjun to be Evil under the theory Felix keeps advancing, he would have had to play Success across two consecutive missions, including one that handed Good a 2-0 match point, purely to earn a seat on the very two-player team he could then fail. That is an extraordinarily patient and costly line of play, and nothing in his behavior supports it — he has been consistent, transparent, and accountable in every discussion. Set that against the alternative Felix is proposing. He has no mission record at all and has voted against both teams that went on to succeed, and he has been upfront that this stems from self-inclusion rather than any evidence against the proposed players. I take him at his word, but swapping a player with two clean results for an unvetted one makes this team strictly riskier — on the mission that could close out the game for Good. This is the strongest team available on the evidence: the two players with the best track record in the game, proposed by one of them. If it fails, Priya and Arjun come under genuine scrutiny and the board reshapes; that accountability is exactly as it should be. But I will not weaken the lowest-risk option on the table based on a hypothetical. Nothing said since my last turn has changed my read, and I will vote to approve Arjun and Priya.

Priya confirms Arjun, Priya. I am keeping the proposed team of Arjun and Priya. We have both delivered clean successes on Missions 1 and 2, and council consensus strongly supports this pairing as our highest-probability path to victory.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 3 succeeds (0 fail cards).
The Assassin names Omar.
Good wins: the Assassin missed Merlin.

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
